lines.text: A formula does not reveal where bonding electrons came from. Dot and cross diagrams let you account for every outer shell electron and distinguish ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding.

Use different symbols for electrons originally supplied by different atoms. For ionic bonding, show electron transfer, then draw separate ions in brackets with charges, for example, M G O contains magnesium two plus and oxide, with eight outer electrons on O. For covalent bonding, place one shared pair between atoms for each single bond, two for a double bond, and three for a triple bond, show remaining lone pairs. A coordinate bond is a shared pair whose two electrons came from one donor atom, the N lone pair of N H three is donated to H plus when N H four plus forms. Check the total valence electron count, adjusting for ion charge. The octet rule has exceptions, B in B F three has six surrounding electrons, P in P C L five has ten, and an odd electron species such as N O has an unpaired electron. Apply the same counting and origin rules to compounds from ionic bonding and molecular shape topics, including ay L two C L six and C O. Foundation bridge, recall the neutral atom valence counts from the periodic table and the meaning of ion charge. Read any stated bonding type or donor direction before choosing a structure, total electrons and local octets are different checks.

Ionic bonding transfers electrons before electrostatic attraction, covalent bonding shares pairs. A coordinate pair is still a covalent pair after it forms. The same electron pair count helps predict molecular shapes.

Ionic, separate bracketed ions with charges and transferred electrons. Covalent, shared pairs between atoms and any lone pairs. Coordinate, both electrons in the pair come from one donor. Check electron totals, allow incomplete octets, expanded octets and odd electrons. Count every electron once in the whole diagram, a shared pair counts around both bonded atoms when checking their shells.
How would your drawings of M G O and N H four plus differ in brackets, charges and the origin of electron pairs?

In forming N H four plus from N H three and H plus, where do the electrons in the new N H pair originate? Both from nitrogen One from each atom Both from hydrogen One from chlorine ay The nitrogen lone pair is donated to H plus, which has no electron to contribute.

Show the outer shell electrons by drawing dot and cross diagrams for part a, M G O, part b, N H three and part c, N H four plus formed when N H three donates a lone pair to H plus. For, a, use dots for electrons originally from O and crosses for electrons originally from magnesium, omit inner shells and show no electrons on magnesium two plus. For part b, and, c, use dots for electrons originally from N and crosses for electrons originally from H. Include all lone pairs and any required brackets and charges.

M G O contains separate magnesium two plus and O2 minus ions after transfer of two electrons from magnesium to O. N H three has three shared N H pairs and one nitrogen lone pair, donation of that lone pair to H plus forms a fourth shared pair in N H four plus, leaving no nitrogen lone pair and an overall plus charge. The dot dot pair records the origin of the coordinate pair, all four N H bonds are equivalent after formation.

Sketch a complete outer shell dot and cross diagram of C O using the conventional coordinate bond construction. Use dots for electrons originally supplied by C and crosses for those supplied by O. Show every shared and lone pair, and label the donor to acceptor direction of the coordinate pair with an arrow. The molecule has no overall charge.

Carbon supplies four and oxygen six valence electrons, giving ten in total. Two ordinary dot cross pairs and one oxygen supplied cross cross pair leave one lone pair on each atom and an octet around each. The symbols record electron origin in this conventional construction, so the coordinate arrow points from O to C.

Each of the two magnesium atoms transfers two outer electrons, so silicon gains four electrons and has eight in its outer shell. The diagram contains two magnesium two plus ions and one silicon four minus ion, giving a total charge of two open bracket plus two close bracket minus four equals zero. The dots and crosses on silicon distinguish its original electrons from the transferred electrons.

N O supplies five plus six equals eleven valence electrons. A double bond, one N lone pair, two O lone pairs and one unpaired N electron account for all eleven, adding an electron to complete the nitrogen octet would change the neutral species.
An odd total cannot be divided entirely into pairs.

three point seven Dot and cross diagrams.
In one breath.
A dot and cross diagram tracks the outer shell electrons supplied by different atoms. It makes electron transfer, ordinary shared pairs and donor supplied coordinate pairs visible.
Key ideas.

A dot and cross diagram uses two symbols to show where valence electrons came from. The symbols are bookkeeping, a dot electron and a cross electron have identical physical properties. Draw only outer shell electrons unless a question asks otherwise. Put a pair between atoms for a covalent bond and pairs not used in bonds beside their atom as lone pairs.

In ionic bonding, electrons transfer and the resulting ions attract electrostatically. Draw each ion separately in square brackets with its charge. For M G O, magnesium loses two electrons and oxygen gains two, the concentration of magnesium to the power of two plus and open square bracket O close square bracket to the power of two minus. Oxygen's eight outer electrons should include its original six and the two transferred electrons. For M G two S I, two magnesium atoms each lose two electrons, so the ions are two magnesium two plus and one silicon four minus. Do not join them with shared pairs.

In covalent bonding, atoms share electron pairs. In N H three, nitrogen makes three N H shared pairs and retains one lone pair. In C O two, each C equals O double bond contains two shared pairs, each oxygen has two lone pairs. A triple bond contains three shared pairs.

A coordinate, dative covalent, bond is a shared pair in which both electrons were supplied by one atom. The nitrogen lone pair in N H three is donated to H plus to make N H four plus. Draw four N H pairs inside brackets labelled plus, distinguish the originally donated pair by using two nitrogen symbols. Once formed, the four N H bonds are equivalent. In C O, the customary dot and cross account has two ordinary shared pairs and one pair donated from O to C. In the ay L two C L six dimer, bridging chlorines donate lone pairs towards electron deficient aluminium atoms.

C O electron check, Count four plus six equals ten valence electrons. Use dots for C and crosses for O, first place two ordinary dot cross shared pairs, then one O supplied cross cross shared pair. The remaining electrons form one dot dot lone pair on C and one cross cross lone pair on O. Thus six electrons are shared and four are in lone pairs, each atom has an octet. The symbols record electron origin in this conventional construction, and the coordinate arrow points from O to C, O yields C.

The octet is a useful check, not an absolute rule. Boron in B F three has six surrounding electrons. Phosphorus in P C L five has an expanded octet of ten. Neutral N O has eleven valence electrons in total, so at least one is unpaired. These cases can appear in questions.
Method.
Count valence electrons from every atom. Add electrons for a negative charge or subtract for a positive charge.
Decide whether the structure contains separate ions or bonded atoms. For ions, show brackets and charges before placing electrons.
Place bonding pairs and then remaining lone or unpaired electrons, preserving dots and crosses to show their origins.
Count the electrons again. Check each H has two, typical second period atoms have eight where appropriate, and the total charge is correct.
M G two S I electron check.

Draw two separate the concentration of magnesium to the power of two plus ions and one the concentration of silicon to the power of four minus ion. Each magnesium transfers two electrons, giving four transferred electrons in total. Around silicon draw eight outer electrons as four pairs, four dots originally from silicon and four crosses transferred from the two magnesium atoms. Do not place shared pairs between the ions, omit the inner shells and show no electrons on the magnesium ions in this convention. Check the charge, two open bracket plus two close bracket minus four equals zero. Only outer shell electrons and correct brackets and charges are required.
Worked example.

Draw N H four plus formed from N H three and H plus. Count five plus four open bracket one close bracket minus one equals eight valence electrons. Three original N H bonds use six, nitrogen's original lone pair supplies the fourth N H bond to H plus. Put four bonding pairs around N in brackets marked plus. There are no lone pairs on N and eight electrons around it.
Traps.
Trap, Join the ions in M G O with a covalent shared pair. Why it's wrong, magnesium transfers two electrons to O. Instead, Show separately charged bracketed ions.
Trap, Show a C gives O coordinate pair in C O. Why it's wrong, The conventional diagram credits oxygen as donor. Instead, Show O gives C for the coordinate pair.
Trap, Force every atom into an octet. Why it's wrong, Electron deficient, expanded octet and odd electron species exist. Instead, Check the total count first.
Exam technique.

For Sketch or Demonstrate, make every outer electron and charge countable. For Explain, state which atom supplies the pair and which accepts it. Label an unusual coordinate pair clearly, a plain line alone hides its origin.
